To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ethanol exposure during development decreases embryo viability, alters brain monoamine levels and decreases phospholipid turnover.
ethanol exposure in the early stages of development causes a significant decrease in embryo viability.

1) ethanol decreases brain dopamine, homovanillic, lysophospholipids, and phospholipid levels, 2) ethanol decreases brain serotonin and 5 hydroxyindole acetic acid levels, 3) ethanol decreases brain phosphatidyl choline and phosphatide ethanolamine levels, 4) ethanol increases embryo mortality, and 5) ethanol decreases spontaneous motility in the chick embryo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of biogenic amine and phospholipid metabolism in the development of acute and chronic ethanol tolerance in the chick embryo.
the effects of ethanol on the chick embryo brain and embryo development.
the role of biogenic amine and phospholipid metabolism in the development of tolerance to ethanol in the chick embryo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ethanol effects on the embryo are complex, involving both acute and long-term effects on the developing nervous system, and that the effects on phospholipids and biogenic aminers are interrelated.
ethanol exposure during development is detrimental to brain function.
ethanol affects monoaminergic neurons and phospholipid metabolism in the brain during embryonic development in a dose-dependent fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

ethanol has a biphasic effect on the chick embryo brain, with acute effects on motility and biogenic aminers, while chronic effects include decreased viability, altered phospholipid turnover, and altered biogenic aminergic systems.
ethanol exposure during development can alter the brain and its functions in ways that may be irreversible.
the brain of a chick embryo is sensitive to ethanol, but that the effects are not as severe as in the adult.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol exposure can lead to long term effects on brain function.
ethanol can cross the blood/brain barrier in the chick embryo and affect brain biogenic amine levels and phospholipid turnover.
the brain of the developing chick embryo may be more vulnerable to the effects of ethanol than previously thought.
